content: 1. Administer ceftriaxone intravenously at a dose of 80–100 mg/kg once daily over 30–60 minutes for a duration of 7–10 days. Alternatively, administer 5 mg/kg once daily. 2. Provide oxygen therapy if the child exhibits respiratory distress or shock. 3. Treat septic shock with a rapid intravenous infusion of 20 mL/kg of normal saline or Ringer’s lactate. Reassess the child’s condition. If shock persists, repeat the fluid bolus up to a total of 60 mL/kg. If the child remains in shock (fluid-refractory shock), initiate adrenaline or dopamine therapy if available. 4. For fever causing distress or discomfort, administer paracetamol or ibuprofen. 5. Monitor hemoglobin (Hb) or packed cell volume (PCV). If indicated, provide a blood transfusion of 20 mL/kg of fresh whole blood or 10 mL/kg of packed cells, adjusting the infusion rate based on the child’s circulatory status. 6. Ensure the child is checked by a nurse at least every 3 hours and by a doctor at least twice daily. Monitor for new complications such as shock, cyanosis, reduced urine output, signs of bleeding (e.g., petechiae, purpura, bleeding from venepuncture sites), or skin ulceration. 7. Consider typhoid fever in children presenting with fever lasting ≥7 days, especially if malaria has been excluded, and if symptoms such as constipation, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, cough, or transient rash are present. In light-skinned children, pink spots on the abdominal wall may be observed. Hepatosplenomegaly or a tender/distended abdomen may also be present. 8. Treat typhoid fever with oral ciprofloxacin at 15 mg/kg twice daily or another fluoroquinolone (e.g., gatifloxacin, ofloxacin, perfloxacin) for 7–10 days. If there is poor response after 48 hours, consider drug-resistant typhoid and switch to second-line antibiotics such as IV ceftriaxone (80 mg/kg/day) or oral azithromycin (20 mg/kg/day) for 5–7 days. Follow national guidelines for local antibiotic resistance patterns. 9. For mastoiditis, administer IV or IM cloxacillin or flucloxacillin at 50 mg/kg every 6 hours or ceftriaxone until improvement, for a total of 10 days. If no response is observed within 48 hours or the condition worsens, refer the child to a surgical specialist for possible incision, drainage, or mastoidectomy. 10. Acute otitis media should be treated with oral amoxicillin at 40 mg/kg twice daily for at least 5 days. If pus is draining from the ear, teach the caregiver how to wick the ear dry three times daily until the discharge ceases. Advise against placing anything in the ear and avoid swimming or water exposure. 11. Chronic otitis media, defined as pus draining from the ear for ≥2 weeks, should be managed with ear wicking and topical antibiotic drops containing quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin) twice daily for 2 weeks. Oral antibiotics are not recommended for chronic ear infections unless systemic infection is present. 12. For urinary tract infections (UTIs), consider the diagnosis in children with fever ≥38°C lasting at least 24 hours without an obvious cause, vomiting, poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, or specific symptoms such as increased frequency or pain during urination. Treat with oral antibiotics for 7–10 days, such as co-trimoxazole (10 mg/kg trimethoprim and 40 mg/kg sulfamethoxazole every 12 hours for 5 days) or alternatives like ampicillin, amoxicillin, or cephalexin, depending on local sensitivity patterns. Encourage fluid intake and treat pain with paracetamol. 13. Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis should be suspected in children with fever, refusal to move the affected limb, or localized swelling and tenderness. Treat with IV cloxacillin or flucloxacillin (50 mg/kg every 6 hours) for children >3 years, or alternatives like clindamycin or third-generation cephalosporins. Transition to oral antibiotics once the fever resolves, continuing treatment for 3 weeks for septic arthritis and 5 weeks for osteomyelitis. In cases of septic arthritis, aspirate the joint to remove pus. If swelling recurs or the infection responds poorly, surgical drainage and debridement may be necessary. 14. Dengue fever should be suspected in children with fever lasting >2 days in endemic areas. Symptoms may include headache, retro-orbital pain, joint and muscle pain, abdominal pain, vomiting, and rash. Encourage oral fluid intake with clean water or oral rehydration solution (ORS). Treat high fever with paracetamol, avoiding aspirin or NSAIDs due to the risk of bleeding. Monitor the child daily for signs of severe disease, such as mucosal bleeding, shock, altered mental status, or jaundice. Admit children with severe disease for further management.
